title: Telemedicine and Triage
answer: Symptom routing, camera-based vital signs, wearables, conversational care and mental health signals.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Symptom Triage and Routing
children.blurb: Symptom triage and routing covers the front door of care: the questions a patient answers about symptoms, the urgency level the system assigns, and the destination it recommends, such as emergency care, urgent care, a telehealth visit, a primary care appointment, or self care at home.

children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Vital signs from a camera refers to software that estimates pulse rate, respiratory rate, and sometimes blood oxygen saturation from subtle color changes and motion in a person's face or chest captured by an ordinary camera.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care covers continuous or intermittent physiological signals collected outside the clinic, such as heart rate, activity, sleep, blood oxygen, glucose, and single-lead electrocardiogram readings, and their use in remote monitoring, triage, and chronic disease management.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care refers to AI systems that interact with patients through text or voice to collect symptoms, answer questions, and support triage before or instead of a human clinician.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health are behavioral and physiological data collected through phones, wearables, and telehealth platforms that may indicate changes in mood, sleep, activity, speech, or social engagement.

sections.body: Telemedicine and Triage is the part of AI medicine that handles first contact, before a clinician sees a patient. It routes symptoms to the right level of care, reads vital signs from a phone camera, pulls data from wearables, and runs text or voice conversations that ask about complaints. In practice, these systems are used in urgent care lines, remote monitoring programs, and direct-to-patient apps. They do not diagnose on their own in most regulated settings, but they can flag red flags, collect history, and decide whether a human should call back. The work is less about replacing doctors and more about sorting, measuring, and watching at a distance.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some pieces are mature. Symptom checkers and routing tools are widely deployed, and camera-based pulse and breathing estimates have improved enough for screening in controlled conditions. Wearable data is now common in cardiology and sleep clinics, though integration into electronic records remains uneven. Conversational agents can handle simple intake and follow-up, but they fail on ambiguity, comorbidity, and emotional nuance. Mental health signal detection from typing, voice, or activity is promising and ethically fraught, with weak validation in many populations. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and only a fraction have been tested in the messy conditions of real telemedicine, so the honest limits remain: no camera or chatbot replaces a physical exam, and false reassurance is a real harm.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from first contact to ongoing observation. Symptom Triage and Routing covers the decision logic that sends a patient to self-care, a virtual visit, or an emergency room. Vital Signs from a Camera explains how ordinary sensors estimate pulse, breathing, and blood pressure proxies, and where those estimates break down. Wearable Data in Clinical Care looks at continuous streams from consumer devices and the work of making them useful to clinicians. Conversational Care and Its Limits examines chat and voice agents for intake, coaching, and follow-up, including what they cannot hear. Digital Signals of Mental Health closes the section with passive and active signals for mood, sleep, and risk, and the privacy questions they raise, so a reader can move through these pages in order or jump to the one that matches a specific deployment question.
